CouchDB replication and versioned backups

Nightly scripts that mirror CouchDB databases from one server to another and keep timestamped snapshots on the target, pruned on a restic-style retention policy (keep 7 daily, 5 weekly, 12 monthly, 7 yearly — or whatever you choose).

What to replicate lives in a CSV inventory that names servers by short aliases. What those aliases mean lives in a servers table, which holds no passwords and is meant to be committed. Passwords live in a separate .env file. None of it is baked into the scripts, so adding a database to the backup set is a one-line config edit, not a code change on every host:

src-svr,targ-svr,rep-svr,db-name,keep
cloud,bak1,bak1,orders,7/5/12/7

Read this before your first live run: versioning deletes databases. Jump to Snapshots and retention and Caveats.

Quick start

# 1. credentials, one entry per server. MUST be chmod 600.
cp repv-env.example /root/couchdb-repv/.repv-env
chmod 600 /root/couchdb-repv/.repv-env
$EDITOR /root/couchdb-repv/.repv-env

# 2. what your server aliases mean. No passwords in here.
cp repv-servers.csv.example /root/couchdb-repv/repv-servers.csv
$EDITOR /root/couchdb-repv/repv-servers.csv

# 3. what to back up
cp repv-inventory.csv.example /root/couchdb-repv/repv-inventory.csv
$EDITOR /root/couchdb-repv/repv-inventory.csv

# 4. does the config even make sense? No network, no changes, instant.
./couchdb-repv.sh \
    --inventory /root/couchdb-repv/repv-inventory.csv \
    --servers   /root/couchdb-repv/repv-servers.csv \
    --env       /root/couchdb-repv/.repv-env \
    --check

# 5. see exactly what it WOULD do - changes nothing
./couchdb-repv.sh \
    --inventory /root/couchdb-repv/repv-inventory.csv \
    --servers   /root/couchdb-repv/repv-servers.csv \
    --env       /root/couchdb-repv/.repv-env \
    --dry-run

# 6. when the plan looks right, drop --dry-run
./couchdb-repv.sh \
    --inventory /root/couchdb-repv/repv-inventory.csv \
    --servers   /root/couchdb-repv/repv-servers.csv \
    --env       /root/couchdb-repv/.repv-env

All three files are named explicitly and none is inferred. Name them whatever suits the job — the tool is not tied to any particular fleet.

Always --check an edited inventory, and dry-run a new one. --check answers "does this config mean what I think it means" in a second with no network; --dry-run answers "what would tonight actually do" and prints the same plan the real run will follow.

Requirements

bash 4+, curl, GNU date, logger, and flock (optional but recommended). No jq, no Python, nothing to install. Deploy by rsyncing the whole directory — the scripts call each other:

rsync -av --exclude '.repv-*' --exclude '.git' ./ root@host:/opt/couchdb-repv/

The three files you write

1. The env file

One _USER and one _PASS per CouchDB server, keyed by hostname or IP — the hostname the alias resolves to, not the alias:

# /root/couchdb-repv/.repv-env   -   chmod 600

couchdb.example.com_USER=admin
couchdb.example.com_PASS=hunter2

203.0.113.10_USER=admin
203.0.113.10_PASS=s3cr3t-with-@-and-#-is-fine

192.168.66.9_USER=admin
192.168.66.9_PASS=another-password
  • chmod 600 is enforced. A group- or world-readable env file is refused outright. Override with --allow-insecure-env only if you have a reason.
  • Values are taken verbatim. A password may contain = # $ { } @ : and spaces. Wrap in quotes if you like — one layer is stripped.
  • Do not put a trailing comment on a value line. PASS=abc # note makes the password abc # note.
  • Blank lines and # lines are ignored. export prefixes and CRLF files are tolerated.

Renaming an alias never touches this file. Moving a server to a new address does.

If two CouchDBs share a box on different ports, a port-qualified key wins over the bare hostname:

192.168.66.9_USER=admin          # everything on this box, unless overridden
192.168.66.9_PASS=another-password
192.168.66.9:6984_USER=other     # just the one on :6984
192.168.66.9:6984_PASS=different

Almost every fleet only ever needs the bare hostname form.

Why not just source it? Because couchdb.example.com_USER contains dots and is not a legal shell variable name. The scripts parse this file themselves and never run eval, so a password containing $(...) stays literal text.

2. The servers table

What each alias means. No credentials, so unlike the env file this one is meant to live in version control:

# /root/couchdb-repv/repv-servers.csv

alias,url
bak1,http://192.168.66.5:5984
bak2,http://192.168.66.11:5984
cloud,http://203.0.113.10:5984

Named by --servers, which is required like the other two. One table can serve every job on a host, or each job can have its own.

  • alias — letters, digits, . _ -.
  • url — scheme://host[:port], no path, and no credentials: a url carrying them is refused, not warned about. The env file is the only source; a second one means two places to look when a password stops working.
  • Name aliases after the box, not the role. The same machine is the targ-svr of one row and the rep-svr of another; SRC_/TARG_/REP_ prefixes force it to appear twice under two names, and the two drift apart.
  • Two aliases may point at one box. The first listed is the one used in logs.
  • A duplicate alias is an error, not last-wins — an accidental duplicate would silently reroute every row naming it, and you would find out at restore time.
  • Any bad entry refuses the whole file. A half-understood server table is not something to run a backup against: the rows that did parse still write to real machines.

Keeping this separate from the env file is the point. When a backup turns out to be missing, "which box was bak1 in August?" has to be answerable from git log — and it cannot be if the topology lives in a 0600 file nobody reads.

3. The inventory CSV

One row per database per target. The header row is authoritative — column order is free, but every column must be present:

src-svr,targ-svr,rep-svr,db-name,keep
cloud,bak1,bak1,app_meta,7/5/12/7
column meaning
src-svr where the data comes from
targ-svr where the mirror and its snapshots live
rep-svr the node that performs the copy — see below
db-name database name, same at both ends
keep retention: daily/weekly/monthly/yearly, or none — see below

The three server columns take an alias from the servers table. Credentials never appear here at all; they are looked up from the env file by the hostname the alias resolves to. An unknown alias stops that row and the error lists the aliases that do exist.

A server column takes an alias and nothing else. A URL written there is read as an alias nobody defined, and the error says so — there is no second accepted form, because a parser with two of them has to explain both.

Mirror without snapshots

Write none in the keep column for a database you want mirrored but never snapshotted:

src-svr,targ-svr,rep-svr,db-name,keep
bak2,bak1,bak1,scratch_db,none

Versioning is not run for that row at all, so nothing is created and — this is the important part — nothing existing is deleted. Switching a database to mirror-only leaves the snapshots it already has exactly where they are; they simply stop being maintained. Delete them by hand if you want the space.

The trade-off is that the target is overwritten each night with no prior state preserved, so a bad day upstream is not recoverable from that target. Every such row logs a MIRROR-ONLY line and the run summary counts them, so it stays visible rather than becoming a silent gap in your backups.

0/0/0/0 is not the same thing and stays refused — zero keeps would select every existing snapshot for deletion. Use none.

none is case-insensitive.

none is the whole policy or none of it. none/5/12/7 is not four integers, so there is no half-sentinel to reject and no error to explain: the state simply cannot be written down.

Blank lines and # lines are skipped. There is no quoting and no escaping: fields are split on commas, which is exact because neither a CouchDB database name nor an alias nor these URLs can contain one. A row whose field count doesn't match the header is rejected and named, never silently misread.

To back one database up to two targets, write two rows.

Picking rep-svr

CouchDB replication is a POST to one node's /_replicate. That node does the work, so it must reach both the source and the target.

  • Usually: the target. It pulls from the source. Set rep-svr = targ-svr.

  • LAN → cloud: the LAN node. A CloudVendor box cannot reach 192.168.x, so it cannot pull. The LAN node must drive the copy:

    # src is on the LAN, target is in the cloud, so the LAN node drives it
src-svr,targ-svr,rep-svr,db-name,keep
bak2,cloud,bak1,ledger_test,7/5/12/7

    Read that row as "from bak2 to cloud, driven by bak1". Aliases are what make this checkable at a glance — spelled out as three credentialled URLs, a wrong rep-svr is invisible on the line.

Getting this wrong shows up as 500 {"error":"db_not_found"} even though the database plainly exists — the replicating node just can't see it.

Running it

couchdb-repv.sh --inventory FILE --servers FILE --env FILE [options]

One invocation per job. Nothing is inferred from anything else, so running a second job is a second command line with its own three files.

option default what it does
--inventory FILE required the CSV of what to replicate
--env FILE required the credentials file
--servers FILE required the alias table
--log-tag TAG this script's name syslog tag; give each cron job its own
--check off resolve the config, print what it means, stop. No lock, no network, no writes
--dry-run true false plan everything, change nothing. Bare --dry-run works too
--sleep SECONDS 1 pause between rows
--max-delete N 8 per-database ceiling on snapshot deletions in one run
--continuous true false live replication instead of one-shot — see Caveats
--strict true false abort the whole run if any row fails preflight
--skip-preflight off skip the pre-run server checks
--timeout SECONDS 60 timeout for metadata requests
--rep-timeout SECONDS 86400 timeout for the copy itself
--dblist-dir DIR off also record each source server's _all_dbs into DIR
--lock-file PATH one per inventory run lock; pass "" to disable
--allow-insecure-env off permit a group/world-readable env file

Common invocations:

# the three files, once, so the rest of these can be short
CFG="--inventory /root/couchdb-repv/repv-inventory.csv \
     --servers   /root/couchdb-repv/repv-servers.csv \
     --env       /root/couchdb-repv/.repv-env"

# does this config mean what I think it means? instant, offline, safe any time
./couchdb-repv.sh $CFG --check

# rehearse an edited inventory
./couchdb-repv.sh $CFG --dry-run

# refuse to run at all if anything is misconfigured
./couchdb-repv.sh $CFG --strict true

# a large database that needs more than an hour to copy is already fine
# (--rep-timeout defaults to 24h); raise it only if you have something bigger
./couchdb-repv.sh $CFG --rep-timeout 172800

Checking the config with --check

The alias table puts one hop between what the inventory says and which machine gets written to. --check is where that hop is made visible — it resolves the inventory, the servers table and the credentials, prints the result, and touches nothing at all:

CHECK: inventory /root/couchdb-repv/repv-inventory.csv
CHECK: servers   /root/couchdb-repv/repv-servers.csv
CHECK:   DATABASE                      SRC     TARG    REP     KEEP
CHECK:   ledger_test         bak2    cloud   bak1    7/5/12/7
CHECK:   aa_orders_candidate  bak2    bak1    bak1    7/5/12/7
CHECK:   orders_test          bak2    bak1    bak1    none
CHECK: servers as resolved
CHECK:   bak1    ->  http://***:***@192.168.66.5:5984
CHECK:   bak2    ->  http://***:***@192.168.66.11:5984
CHECK:   cloud   ->  http://***:***@203.0.113.10:5984
CHECK: 3 usable row(s), 0 rejected
CHECK: inventory is usable - nothing was changed

The redacted URL is the useful half of that legend: http://***:***@host says credentials were found and attached, http://host says none were.

It takes no run lock, so it is safe while last night's job is still going, and it makes no network calls, so it says nothing about whether those servers are actually up — that is what --dry-run and preflight are for. Exit 0 if every row is usable, 1 if any row was rejected, 2 if the header is wrong. That makes it usable as a pre-deploy gate.

Order of operations

For every row, in this order:

  1. Snapshot the target as it currently stands, then prune old snapshots.
  2. Replicate the source over the target.

Versioning runs first on purpose: it preserves the last known-good target state before the mirror overwrites it, so a bad day upstream stays recoverable.

It follows that if versioning fails, that row is not replicated. Overwriting a target whose previous state could not be preserved is exactly what turns a bad day into data loss. You'll see:

ERROR: ROW 4: SKIP replicate app_meta: versioning failed, refusing to overwrite
       192.168.66.5:5984/app_meta with its previous state unpreserved

The one exception is a target database that doesn't exist yet — there's no history to protect, so it replicates normally and logs SKIP no target database ... yet.

What a run looks like

Output goes to the screen and to syslog, under the script's own name. Real output from a healthy run:

Every KEEP line says why that snapshot survived, so a surprising survivor can always be explained from the log.

The per-database summary

Every run ends with one line per processed row, in inventory order:

FIN: per-database summary
FIN:   DATABASE     SOURCE              TARGET              VERSIONS   DOCS UPD    TIME
FIN:   orders       192.168.66.30:5984  192.168.66.31:5984         1          2      6s   1 snapshot(s) pruned
FIN:   app_meta     192.168.66.30:5984  192.168.66.31:5984         1          0      7s   already current
FIN:   orders_test  192.168.66.30:5984  192.168.66.31:5984         -          0      4s   mirror-only, no snapshots
FIN:   orders_test  192.168.66.31:5984  192.168.66.30:5984         0          9      5s   first copy, nothing to snapshot yet
column meaning
DATABASE database name. Not unique — the same database replicated to two targets is two rows.
SOURCE which server this row read from.
TARGET which server this row wrote to. SOURCE and TARGET together are what tell those two rows apart.
VERSIONS snapshots of this database now kept on that target. - means the row is mirror-only (keep is none), so no snapshot is ever taken.
DOCS UPD documents this run actually wrote. 0 with already current means the target was up to date — not that the row was skipped.
TIME wall-clock for the whole row, versioning plus replication. Excludes --sleep, which is pacing, not work.

DOCS UPD is not docs_read/docs_written. Those are cumulative lifetime totals for the replication and a run that copies nothing replays the previous session's history verbatim, so they read identically on a busy run and an idle one. DOCS UPD is derived: CouchDB's no_changes flag when it did nothing, and otherwise this history entry's total minus the previous one's. It counts updates as well as insertions, so it moves even when doc_count does not.

A run with pruning:

INFO: retention: 2 kept, 5 to delete (of 7 snapshots)
INFO: DELETE app_meta_snap_20260823-020500 on 192.168.66.31:5984: http=200
INFO: DELETE app_meta_snap_20260820-020500 on 192.168.66.31:5984: http=200
...
INFO: FIN: app_meta on 192.168.66.31:5984: snapshot 20260825-132356, 2 kept, 5 deleted, 0 delete(s) FAILED

Reading the logs

# this job, today
journalctl -t repv --since today

# just the failures
journalctl -t repv --since today | grep ERROR

# the end-of-run summary
journalctl -t repv --since today | grep 'FIN:'

# on a host without journald
grep repv /var/log/syslog | grep ERROR

Match on ERROR, not on HTTP status. CouchDB reports most replication problems as 500, not 4xx — a missing source database comes back as 500 {"error":"db_not_found"}.

Passwords never appear. Every log line is redacted: http://admin:hunter2@h prints as http://***:***@h, on screen and in syslog.

Snapshots and retention

Each run copies the target database to a timestamped snapshot on the same server:

app_meta                          the live mirror
app_meta_snap_20260825-020501     today
app_meta_snap_20260824-020458     yesterday
app_meta_snap_20260731-020502     end of July
app_meta_snap_20251231-020455     end of 2025

Then it deletes the snapshots outside your keep policy — the same selection restic forget makes.

How the policy actually works

Walking newest to oldest, a snapshot is kept when it opens a new bucket of a type that still has keeps left. Buckets are the day, the ISO week, the month and the year. A snapshot survives if any of the four keeps it.

Two consequences that surprise people:

  • These are not "the last N days". They're the last N snapshots that start a new day/week/month/year. A gap in the series does not burn a keep — if you didn't run for a fortnight, a daily keep of 7 still holds seven snapshots, just older ones.
  • Several runs in one day collapse to one snapshot. Only the newest snapshot of a given day counts as that day's daily, so a mid-day re-run is safe: it replaces the morning's snapshot rather than consuming a second slot.

7,5,12,7 settles at about 31 snapshots per database. Every snapshot is a full copy, so budget disk accordingly.

When it will not delete

Nothing is deleted unless all of these hold:

  • A new snapshot was created and verified — HTTP 200, "ok":true, doc_write_failures:0, and its doc_count matches the live database. No good new snapshot means no deletions at all, ever.
  • The name matches <db>_snap_<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS> exactly. Nothing else is even a candidate.
  • It isn't the live database, the snapshot just taken, or a _users / _replicator style system database.
  • The newest snapshot always survives, and at least one snapshot always survives.
  • The count doesn't exceed --max-delete (default 8).

The --max-delete ceiling is a circuit breaker. Steady state is 0–2 deletions a night, so a bigger number means the clock, the policy or the listing is wrong:

ERROR: refusing to delete 47 snapshots of app_meta in one run: --max-delete is 8
ERROR: review the list with --dry-run true, then raise --max-delete deliberately if it is correct

Do exactly that — --dry-run true prints the full list even when the ceiling trips — and only then raise it:

./couchdb-repv-version.sh --rep-svr URL --targ-svr URL --db-name app_meta \
    --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 5 --keep-monthly 12 --keep-yearly 7 \
    --dry-run true                    # what would go?

Timing: a snapshot is one cycle behind

Versioning runs before replication, so app_meta_snap_20260825-020501 holds the target as it stood after the 24 August run, not the 25th. That's the point — it's the copy you reach for when the 25th brought something bad. The stamp is when the snapshot was taken, not the age of the data in it.

Restoring from a snapshot

There's no restore script; a restore is a judgement call, not a cron job. The mechanics are one curl. Always restore to a new name first and inspect it.

TARG='http://admin:PASSWORD@192.168.66.5:5984'

# 1. what do I have?
curl -s "$TARG/_all_dbs" | tr ',' '\n' | grep app_meta

# 2. how big is the snapshot I want?
curl -s "$TARG/app_meta_snap_20260824-020458" | head -c 300

# 3. restore it alongside the live database, NOT over it
curl -X POST "$TARG/_replicate" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "source": "'"$TARG"'/app_meta_snap_20260824-020458",
  "target": "'"$TARG"'/app_meta_restored",
  "create_target": true,
  "continuous": false
}'

# 4. check it, then swap it in yourself when you are satisfied
curl -s "$TARG/app_meta_restored" | head -c 300

If you're restoring because the source is bad, comment that row out of the inventory first, or the next nightly run will replicate the bad data straight back over your work.

The component scripts

The nightly job is built from two standalone scripts you can also run by hand on a single database. Useful for one-offs, for testing, and for recovery.

couchdb-repv-version.sh — snapshot and prune one database

./couchdb-repv-version.sh \
    --rep-svr  http://admin:pw@192.168.66.5:5984 \
    --targ-svr http://admin:pw@192.168.66.5:5984 \
    --db-name  app_meta \
    --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 5 --keep-monthly 12 --keep-yearly 7 \
    --dry-run true

Snapshots are target-to-target — the backup host copies from itself — so there's no --src-svr. Options: --max-delete N (default 8), --timeout, --rep-timeout, --dry-run.

couchdb-repv-replicate.sh — copy one database

./couchdb-repv-replicate.sh \
    --rep-svr  http://admin:pw@192.168.66.5:5984 \
    --src-svr  http://admin:pw@203.0.113.10:5984 \
    --targ-svr http://admin:pw@192.168.66.5:5984 \
    --db-name  app_meta

Options: --continuous true|false (default false), --create-target true|false (default true), --timeout, --rep-timeout, --dry-run.

Credentials typed on a command line land in your shell history and in ps output. For anything routine, use the inventory.

Cron

5 2 * * * /opt/couchdb-repv/couchdb-repv.sh --log-tag repv --inventory /root/couchdb-repv/repv-inventory.csv --servers /root/couchdb-repv/repv-servers.csv --env /root/couchdb-repv/.repv-env

Give each job its own --log-tag. It is what separates two jobs in syslog, and without it they both log under couchdb-repv.sh and interleave.

The scripts exit 1 if anything failed, so with MAILTO= set, cron mails you on a bad night and stays quiet on a good one. Everything is in syslog either way.

Each inventory gets its own lock, so these two don't block each other even though they fire in the same minute. A run that overruns into the next night's slot is refused rather than doubled up:

ERROR: another run holds /tmp/couchdb-repv-...lock - exiting rather than running two at once

Suggested rollout: put the job in cron with --dry-run true for a week first, read the mail it sends, and drop the flag only once the plan it prints looks right every night.

Caveats, read these

Versioning deletes databases. That's the whole point of a retention policy, but it is a delete. The guards above make it hard to delete the wrong thing — they can't make it impossible to delete the right thing under a policy you didn't mean. Dry-run any policy change.

The mirror is one-shot, not live. Replication runs at 02:05 and finishes. The target is as fresh as the last run, not live. If you look at a backup at 4pm you're seeing this morning. --continuous true switches to live replication, but then HTTP 202 only means accepted — the job can still fail asynchronously, and you have to check _scheduler/jobs to know it's healthy.

Snapshots are full copies on the same server. No deduplication, no compression, and no protection against that server dying. This is version history, not offsite backup — you still want a cold copy of the target's data directory somewhere else.

doc_count is not a checksum. The snapshot check catches a truncated or failed copy. It does not prove document-level equality.

Deleted documents don't reduce doc_count until the tombstone replicates, so an occasional WARN: target doc_count=41 differs from source doc_count=42 is normal, not a failure. Persistent or growing drift is worth looking into.

A row backing up to two targets is two rows, and each keeps its own snapshots on its own target.

A mirror-only row has no snapshot protection. keep of none mirrors without versioning, which means the target is overwritten nightly with nothing preserved beforehand. That is a reasonable thing to want; be deliberate about it.

A database named like a snapshot will be treated as one. Don't create a real database called something_snap_20260825-020501.

Don't run two jobs from one inventory — the lock will refuse the second. Split the inventory instead.

Timestamps are local time. Around a daylight-saving change a day may hold two snapshots or none. Retention handles both correctly; the bucket just moves.

Troubleshooting

env file ... is mode 644; it holds passwords and must not be group/other readable → chmod 600 the env file.

server alias 'bak1' (192.168.66.5:5984) has no credentials: the env file needs 192.168.66.5_USER and 192.168.66.5_PASS → Add exactly those two keys. The env file is keyed by the hostname the alias resolves to, never by the alias itself.

unknown server alias 'bak1' - the servers file defines: cloud bak2 bak1 → A typo in the inventory, or an alias you never added to the servers table.

unknown server alias 'http://admin:pw@host:5984' → A URL where an alias belongs. Server columns hold aliases only: add the server to the servers table and write its alias here.

--servers is required → All three files are named explicitly. There is no inferred path.

servers file ...: 1 bad entr(ies) - refusing to run → Unlike a bad inventory row, a bad servers entry stops everything. The rows that did parse still write to real machines, so a half-understood table is not something to proceed on. Fix the line it names.

header is missing column(s): keep → The header row is authoritative and this one has no keep column. Retention is one column: 7/5/12/7, or none.

keep: daily must be a non-negative integer, got 'none' in 'none/5/12/7' → In the single-column form, none means the whole policy. There is no partial form — write none, or four numbers.

inventory line 4: has 4 fields, header has 5 → A missing or extra comma on that line. The row is rejected rather than guessed at, which is deliberate — a shifted field would put a retention count where a database name should be.

keep: 0/0/0/0 would select every existing snapshot for deletion → Zero keeps would select every snapshot for deletion, so it is refused. If you meant "mirror but never snapshot", write none.

servers file ... line 2: 'bak1' has credentials in its url → Credentials belong in the --env file, keyed by hostname. The servers table is meant to be committed.

header is missing column(s): rep-svr → Add it — see Picking rep-svr.

http=401: {"error":"unauthorized","reason":"Name or password is incorrect."} → Wrong credentials for that host. Preflight catches this before anything is written. --check will not: it makes no network calls, and a resolved http://***:***@host only means credentials were found, not that they work.

500 {"error":"db_not_found"} but the database exists → Almost always rep-svr pointing at a node that can't reach the source. Check from that node: curl -s http://user:pw@SOURCE:5984/dbname.

SKIP replicate ...: versioning failed → Working as designed. Fix the versioning error above it — the target is untouched, and nothing was deleted.

refusing to delete 47 snapshots ... --max-delete is 8 → Review with --dry-run true, then raise --max-delete if the list is right.

another run holds /tmp/couchdb-repv-....lock → Last night's run is still going, or died leaving the lock held. Check with ps aux | grep couchdb-rep.

Timed out after 86400s → The copy is probably still running server-side. Check curl -s http://user:pw@REPSVR:5984/_scheduler/jobs before retrying — a blind retry stacks up duplicate jobs.

Exit codes

code meaning
0 everything succeeded
1 something failed — the FIN: lines list what
2 usage or config error — bad flag, missing column, unreadable file
3 (couchdb-repv-version.sh only) nothing to snapshot; the target database doesn't exist yet

Tests

tests/run-all.sh --unit     # lint + unit only. No network, no config, no setup.
tests/run-all.sh            # the above, then the live integration suite
tests/integration.sh keep   # run, then leave the test databases in place
tests/integration.sh teardown

The integration suite needs two CouchDB servers that you provide. There is no default and no bundled fixture: it will not start until you have written both files, so it cannot run against whatever happens to be on the network.

cp repv-test-servers.csv.example .repv-test-servers.csv   # test0 and test1
$EDITOR .repv-test-servers.csv

cp repv-test-env.example .repv-test-env
chmod 600 .repv-test-env                                   # refused otherwise
$EDITOR .repv-test-env

Or point CDB_TEST_SERVERS / CDB_TEST_ENV elsewhere. Both files are gitignored, and both use the tool's own formats, read by the tool's own parsers.

These two servers must be disposable. The suite creates and deletes databases on them. It only ever touches names prefixed zz_test_, and only on the two hosts that table names — but the code doing the deleting is the code under test. Use scratch containers or throwaway VMs, with credentials that are not reused anywhere, and never point it at anything holding data you'd miss.

repv-test-inventory.csv.example is there for a manual smoke run — --check, then --dry-run, then a real run — before you trust the same three files against a fleet that matters. The suite does not read it; it generates its own.

The unit tests need only bash and GNU date, and cover the two things that decide what happens to real data with nothing in the way:

  • test-retention.sh — retention_select, the one piece of code that deletes. Written as a pure function precisely so it can be tested with no CouchDB in the way.
  • test-inventory.sh — the servers table, alias resolution, credential derivation and the keep grammar. An alias is what decides which machine gets written to, so it gets the same treatment.
  • test-env.sh — env parsing, token expansion, URL handling, redaction.
  • test-docs.sh — that README.html was rendered from this README.md. See This README.

The integration suite replicates test0 → test1 and refuses to touch any host that is not one of those two. Every database it creates is prefixed zz_test_, which is also the only prefix teardown removes. It covers the ordering interlock, retention over 200 backdated snapshots, the delete ceiling, the run lock, and failure injection for bad credentials, a missing source database and an unreachable rep-svr.

This README

README.html is a generated file — a self-contained rendering of this README.md for reading in a browser. The CSS is inlined and nothing is fetched at view time, so it opens from a file:// path on a machine with no network, which is the situation you are usually in when you need it.

tools/render-readme.sh            # regenerate README.html from README.md
tools/render-readme.sh --check    # is README.html current?

Any change to README.md must be re-rendered in the same commit. Don't edit README.html by hand — the next render discards the edit without saying so.

tests/test-docs.sh fails when the two have drifted, so tests/run-all.sh --unit catches a README edit committed without a re-render. That failure is worth having: nothing breaks when the HTML goes stale, it just carries on confidently describing how the scripts used to work.

Rendering needs pandoc (apt install pandoc). --check doesn't — it compares a source-sha256: stamp in the HTML against the Markdown, so the check still runs on a host that can't render, rather than being skipped there and quietly ceasing to be a check.

Command reference

couchdb-repv.sh              the entry point: run this
couchdb-repv-version.sh      snapshot + prune ONE database
couchdb-repv-replicate.sh    copy ONE database
couchdb-repv-common.sh       shared library (sourced, not run)

Config files, none of which are code:

repv-servers.csv             alias -> url. No passwords. Safe to commit.
repv-inventory.csv           what to replicate and how long to keep it
.repv-env                    passwords, 0600, never committed

Those are the names the shipped .example files copy to; call them whatever suits the job, since all three are passed explicitly.

Every one of them takes --help (except couchdb-repv-common.sh, which is a library — it is sourced, never run).

./couchdb-repv.sh --help
./couchdb-repv-version.sh --help
